extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, law students, and news‑agency executives concerned with unfair competition and news misappropriation
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and industry criteria for when a rival news service's acquisition and publication of another agency's dispatches constitutes unfair competition, misappropriation, fraud, or justifiable newsgathering. Focuses on methods of acquisition, attribution, knowledge, contractual obligations of members, evidence, and equitable remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreptitious employment to induce contract breach
rubrics_metrics.description: They employed a man surreptitiously to get members to break their contract (e.g., paying editors to telephone out dispatches secretly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret payments or clandestine appointments to induce a member of a news agency to give away news to a competitor are indicia of wrongdoing; the transcript cites payments of $5/week, private telephone‑booth calls, and covert arrangements as evidence of improper inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of compensation to correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish payments made 'for prompt service' of news the payer is entitled to from payments made to obtain local news the correspondent was contractually obligated to furnish to another agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments made openly and with managers' knowledge to secure prompt transmission of news that the payer legitimately receives are defensible; payments intended to procure news to which the payer had no right (i.e., proprietary member news) are wrongful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness versus secrecy of transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether news was delivered openly from the newspaper office or secretly (e.g., via private phone calls) is relevant to assessing honesty of the arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open, above‑board transmissions (sent from the office, known to managers) weigh against misconduct; secret, surreptitious methods suggest dishonest appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct copying from wire outputs (Morkrum machines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors or agents coming to view and copy the sheets printed by another agency's receiving machines (Morkrum) and taking extracts or copies for transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witness testimony that rival editors repeatedly inspected or copied machine‑printed sheets supports a finding of appropriation; identical wording and even identical mistakes in published dispatches serve as strong evidence of copying rather than independent acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying from bulletin boards and early editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically copying dispatches verbatim from bulletin boards or from early editions of newspapers and using them in a competing service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While anyone may view publicly posted bulletins for information, lifting them verbatim and selling them as one's own competitive product is treated as a qualitatively different act and may be enjoined; the court considers whether the competitor merely used tips or reproduced the material wholesale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent investigation versus wholesale appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible practice: learning of a rumor or seeing an early edition and then investigating independently and writing one's own dispatch; impermissible: 'bodily' taking another agency's despatches and selling them as one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following tips and conducting independent verification and original reporting is acceptable; reproducing the other agency's finished work without independent sourcing is actionable unfair competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution/credit to the original source
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the competitor gives credit to The Associated Press (or original source) for the news copied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant acknowledges the source (gives credit), that may permit use of the news; lack of attribution and presenting the dispatches as the competitor's own is a factor in finding unfairness and deception. The transcript suggests enforcing member by‑laws requiring credit as a practical remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of source as enforcement element
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the defendant knew or should have known that the news originated with the plaintiff agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving the competitor's knowledge that the material was plaintiff's news strengthens the equitable case; absence of knowledge may make enforcement and injunctions difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inapplicability or limits of copyright law for raw news
rubrics_metrics.description: The copyright statute is impractical for routine news dispatches (daily multiplicity) and therefore is not the sole or sufficient legal basis to address the harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because customary copyright mechanisms don't protect ephemeral news items effectively, courts consider unfair competition/equity principles to prevent misappropriation even where copyright remedies are unavailable or impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deception/fraud on the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Selling another agency's gathered news as one's own is misleading to the public and constitutes a fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting copied dispatches as if gathered independently deceives readers/customers and is cited as moral and legal wrongdoing supporting injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic harm and unjust enrichment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking news 'which has cost [plaintiff] enormous expense' and selling it as the defendant's own deprives the plaintiff of commercial value and causes unfair competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment centers on commercial impact: appropriation that allows a rival to sell equivalent news cheaper or to divert advertising revenue is an important factor for equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent/nature of copying (word‑for‑word reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproducing an entire newspaper or dispatches word‑for‑word (e.g., duplicating the Evening Post with different masthead) is especially egregious and 'shocking to the moral sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of verbatim replication (entire pages or wholesale copying) intensifies the unfairness analysis and supports injunctive relief; even if publicity/advertising claims are truthful, the imitation of another's product undermines fair competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry custom as a mitigating/limiting factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Customary practices (tips, rumors, casual gleaning) by news agencies are recognized as part of competitive newsgathering, but do not justify wholesale copying of another agency's prepared dispatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court distinguishes ordinary newsgathering customs (permitted when followed by independent reporting) from systematic appropriation schemes; custom alone does not legalize conduct that amounts to misappropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and weight of evidence (affidavits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative probative value of affidavits: testimony by disinterested employees who directly observed copying may carry more weight than denials by interested managers seeking to preserve membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate witness interest and directness of observation; corroborating affidavits (telephone operators, machine attendants) strengthen claims of systematic copying or surreptitious conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of equitable relief (injunction) for misappropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of equity has the power to enjoin appropriation of news by unfair means; equitable relief is sought to stop competitors from 'reaping where they have not sown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unfair competition, deception, or appropriation causing irreparable harm is shown, the transcript asserts that injunctive relief is an appropriate remedy even where copyright law is inadequate.
